title: The Taxi Driver's Daughter
author: Léxi
desc: À Abidjan, Awa aide son père chauffeur de woro-woro… et découvre un secret dans le taxi.

p: Every morning at five o'clock, Awa hears the same sound. Her father's orange taxi starts in front of the house. Vroom, vroom, cough, cough. The old car is tired, but it always starts.

Her father is called Moussa. He drives a woro-woro, a shared taxi, in Abidjan. He goes from Adjamé to Plateau, from Plateau to Cocody, all day long. He knows every street, every hole in the road, every seller at every corner.
Awa is fifteen. She wants to be a doctor one day. But this year, there is a problem. School costs money, and her father's taxi is getting old. Every week, something breaks.
"Papa, can I come with you on Saturday?" Awa asks one evening.
Her father laughs. "In the taxi? A taxi is not a place for a future doctor."
"Please. I want to help. I can count the money. I can call the passengers."
He looks at her for a long time. Then he smiles. "OK. Saturday. Five o'clock. Don't be late."

On Saturday, Awa sits in the front seat. The sun is not up yet, but the streets are already full of people. Women carry big bowls on their heads. Men drink coffee in small plastic cups. Children run to the bus station.
"Adjamé! Plateau! Plateau!" Awa shouts from the window.
The taxi fills up quickly. A student with a big bag. An old woman with a chicken in a basket. A man in a suit, talking on two phones at the same time.
"How much to Plateau, little girl?" asks the man in the suit.
"Three hundred francs, sir," says Awa.
He gives her a thousand-franc note. She gives him seven hundred francs back, fast and correct. Her father looks at her in the mirror and nods. He is proud.

All morning, they drive. Awa learns many things. She learns that the old woman with the chicken goes to see her daughter every Saturday. She learns that the student wants to be an engineer. She learns that every passenger has a story.
At noon, they stop to eat attiéké and fish at a small maquis. Her father counts the money.
"It's a good day," he says. "You bring luck, Awa."
In the afternoon, a young man gets out at Cocody. He runs away fast, because he is late. Awa turns around and sees something on the back seat. A black bag.
"Papa! He forgot his bag!"
Her father stops the car. Awa opens the bag. Inside, there are papers, a laptop, and an envelope. In the envelope, there is a lot of money. More money than her father makes in three months.
Nobody speaks. The car is very quiet.
Awa thinks about her school. She thinks about the old taxi. She thinks about her dream of becoming a doctor. With this money, everything can be easy.
Then she looks at her father. He is looking at her too.
"What do we do, Awa?" he asks softly.
Awa takes a deep breath. "We give it back, Papa. It isn't ours."
Her father smiles. It is the biggest smile she has ever seen on his face.
"That's my daughter," he says.
In the bag, there is a small card with a name and an address: Mr. Kouamé Yao, Director, Riviera 3.
They drive to Riviera 3. It is a big white building with a guard at the door. The guard does not want to let them in. "Taxi drivers wait outside," he says.
But Awa does not give up. "Please tell Mr. Kouamé that we have his black bag."
Five minutes later, a man runs down the stairs. It is the young man from the taxi! He is not the director. He is the director's son, Serge. He looks very afraid.
"My bag! My father's money for the workers! I thought it was lost forever!"
He opens the envelope and counts. Everything is there.
Then an older man comes down the stairs. He is Mr. Kouamé himself. He listens to the story. He looks at Awa and at her father for a long time.
"In Abidjan, many people would keep this money," he says. "Why didn't you?"
Awa answers simply: "Because one day I want to be a doctor. And a doctor must be honest."
Mr. Kouamé is quiet for a moment. Then he takes a pen.
"My company needs a driver for our new minibus," he says to Moussa. "A good salary, a new vehicle, and Sundays free. Do you want the job?"
Moussa can't speak. He just nods. His eyes are wet.
"And you, young lady," says Mr. Kouamé to Awa. "Our company has a scholarship for good students. Bring me your school results on Monday."
On the way home, the old orange taxi coughs more than ever. Vroom, cough, cough, vroom. But nobody cares. Awa and her father sing loudly with the radio.
That night, Awa writes in her notebook:
*Today I learned that every passenger has a story. And that our story is written by the choices we make.*
Two years later, when Awa starts medical school, her father drives her there. In a new white minibus. On the back window, there is a small sticker. It says: *Honest roads lead far.*
